**Daidō Moriyama** ([Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"): 森山 大道, [Hepburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepburn_romanization "Hepburn romanization"): _Moriyama Daidō[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido\_Moriyama#cite\_note-1)_; born October 10, 1938) is a Japanese photographer best known for his black-and-white [street photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_photography "Street photography") and association with the avant-garde photography magazine _[Provoke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provoke\_(magazine) "Provoke (magazine)")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-2)

Moriyama began his career as an assistant to photographer [Eikoh Hosoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eikoh_Hosoe "Eikoh Hosoe"), a co-founder of the avant-garde photo cooperative [Vivo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivo_(photography) "Vivo (photography)"), and made his mark with his first photobook _Japan: A Photo Theater_, published in 1968. His formative work in the 1960s boldly captured the darker qualities of urban life in postwar Japan in rough, unfettered fashion, filtering the rawness of human experience through sharply tilted angles, grained textures, harsh contrast, and blurred movements through the photographer's wandering gaze. Many of his well-known works from the 1960s and 1970s are read through the lenses of post-war reconstruction and [post-Occupation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-occupation_Japan "Post-occupation Japan") cultural upheaval.

Moriyama continued to experiment with the representative possibilities offered by the camera in his 1969 _Accident_ series, which was serialized over one year in the photo magazine _[Asahi Camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asahi\_Camera "Asahi Camera")_, in which he deployed his camera as a copying machine to reproduce existing media images. His 1972 photobook _Farewell Photography_, which was accompanied by an interview with his fellow _Provoke_ photographer [Takuma Nakahira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takuma_Nakahira "Takuma Nakahira"), presents his radical effort to dismantle the medium.

Although the [photobook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photobook "Photobook") is a favored format of presentation among Japanese photographers, Moriyama was particularly prolific: he has produced more than 150 photobooks since 1968. His creative career has been honored by a number of solo exhibitions by major institutions, along with his two-person exhibition with [William Klein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Klein_(photographer) "William Klein (photographer)") at [Tate Modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Modern "Tate Modern") in 2012–13. He has received numerous accolades throughout his career, including the [Hasselblad Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasselblad_Award "Hasselblad Award") in 2019 and the [International Center of Photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Center_of_Photography "International Center of Photography") Infinity Award in 2012.

### Early life and career beginnings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daid%C5%8D_Moriyama&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life and career beginnings")]

Moriyama was born in [Ikeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ikeda,_Osaka "Ikeda, Osaka"), [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka_Prefecture "Osaka Prefecture") in 1938 as Hiromichi Moriyama.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-3) Owing to his father's work, his family moved frequently, and Moriyama spent parts of his childhood in [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo"), [Hiroshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima "Hiroshima"), [Chiba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiba_Prefecture "Chiba Prefecture"), and [Shimane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shimane_Prefecture "Shimane Prefecture") (his paternal family's home prefecture) before returning to Osaka around the age of 11.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Moriyama-2007-4):208

From the ages of 16 to 20, he worked in graphic design before pivoting to photography in his early 20s after purchasing an inexpensive [Canon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canon_Inc. "Canon Inc.") IV Sb from a friend.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Nakamoto-2019-5) In Osaka, Moriyama worked at the studio of photographer [Takeji Iwamiya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takeji_Iwamiya "Takeji Iwamiya") before moving to Tokyo in 1961 to connect with the radical photography collective Vivo, whose work he admired.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Holborn-2004-7):73 He eventually found work as an assistant to photographer and Vivo member [Eikoh Hosoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eikoh_Hosoe "Eikoh Hosoe"), whom he credits with teaching him much of the fundamentals of photographic practice and technique.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Charrier-2010-8):270[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Moriyama-2007-4):207 Yet for the three years he spent working for Hosoe, Moriyama did not take any photographs of his own until Hosoe, out of impatience, urged him to show him some of his own work.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Moriyama-2007-4):207

As a young man coming of age in 1950s and '60s, Moriyama bore witness to the political unrest (illustrated most vividly in the 1960 [Anpo protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anpo_protests "Anpo protests")), economic revival and mass consumerism, and radical art-making that characterized the two decades following the end of World War II. His first photobook, _Nippon gekijō shashinchō_ (にっぽん劇場写真帖, _Japan: A Photo Theater_), published in 1968, captures the excitement, tension, anxiety, and rage of urban life during this critical historical juncture through a collection of images, indiscriminate in subject matter, presented in dizzying succession through full-page spreads. The photographs range from ordinary streetscapes featuring blurred faces and garish signage to snapshots alluding to the aggressive redevelopment taking place in Tokyo and the rubble left in its wake, as well as images of nightlife and darker elements of urban life. As the title of the photobook suggests, Moriyama's approach homes in on the spectacle of everyday life in all its ugliness and splendor.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-9)

In 1965, a series of photographs of preserved human embryos, titled _Mugon geki_ ("silent theatre", _Pantomime_), by Moriyama were published in the magazine _Gendai no me_ and caught the attention of avant-garde poet [Shūji Terayama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sh%C5%ABji_Terayama "Shūji Terayama").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Charrier-2010-8):269–70 Terayama commissioned Moriyama to provide accompanying images for his experimental theatre and prose works, providing Moriyama with a boost in his early career and connecting him to other avant-garde creatives including [Tadanori Yokoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadanori_Yokoo "Tadanori Yokoo") and [Takuma Nakahira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takuma_Nakahira "Takuma Nakahira").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Charrier-2010-8):270 His connection to Nakahira, a founding member of the photography magazine _Provoke,_ eventually led to his participation in the publication beginning with the second issue in 1969.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-world-through-my-eyes-10)

Moriyama is widely recognized for his work associated with the short-lived but deeply influential magazine, which was founded by photographers [Takuma Nakahira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takuma_Nakahira "Takuma Nakahira") and [Yutaka Takanishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yutaka_Takanashi "Yutaka Takanashi"), along with critic [Kōji Taki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C5%8Dji_Taki "Kōji Taki") and writer Takahiko Okada in 1968.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-moma-11) The publication popularized the "are, bure, [boke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bokeh "Bokeh")" style, translated as "grainy/rough, [blurry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blur_(photographic_effect)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Blur (photographic effect) (page does not exist)"), out-of-focus," an aesthetic rebuttal to the dominant European-style photojournalism style (exemplified by [Ken Domon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Domon "Ken Domon")'s realist approach) and straightforward commercial work that dominated the Japanese photography scene at the time.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-moma-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Forbes-2016-12):243 These visions of everyday life rejected the notion that photography captures a lucid reflection of the world undergirded by a legible ideological argument; rather, they sought to emphasize the fragmentary nature of reality and make evident the photographer's prowling, wandering gaze.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Forbes-2016-12):243

Eroticism and masculinized subjectivity are often associated with Moriyama's contributions to the magazine, as evidenced by works such as "Eros" (1969), featured in the second issue of the publication.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-13) The grainy, skewed image features a nude woman smoking a cigarette on a hotel bed—suggestive of the aftermath of a tryst. Her back faces the viewer, while her surroundings are shrouded in dense shadows, giving the camera's gaze a furtive and ominous air.

As stated in the magazine's 1968 manifesto, "[T]he images [_eizō_] themselves are not ideas. They do not possess the wholeness of concepts, neither are they a communicative code like language....But this irreversible materiality [_hikagyakuteki bussitsusei_] – reality cut off from the camera – constitutes the reverse side of the world defined by language; and for this reason, [the image] is at times able to provoke the world of language and ideas."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Kim-2016-14):232–233 _Provoke_ sought to assert photography's role in producing a phenomenological encounter that focused on the bodily and the immediate, moving beyond preconceived notions of truth, reality, and vision to probe questions surrounding the identity of photographic matter and the roles of the photographer, subject, and viewer. Though the collective only produced three issues and a book, _First, Abandon the World of Pseudocertainty – Thoughts on Photography and Language_ (1970), each member continued to publicize their work in close relation to the "era of Provoke," and the magazine has had an immense cultural impact and been the subject of numerous international exhibitions.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Kim-2016-14):232

### _Akushidento_ (Accident) (1969)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daid%C5%8D_Moriyama&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Akushidento (Accident) (1969)")]

In 1968, Moriyama began producing a series focused on the theme of "equivalence" using images featured in mass media as his source material.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Fukugawa-2012-15) According to Moriyama, the series was prompted by an experience he had at a train terminal in Tokyo, whereupon he was shocked to see the news of [Robert F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy "Robert F. Kennedy")'s assassination on the front page of newspapers scattered all around him.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Moriyama-2016-16):392 Taking interest in the mediated nature of press images, Moriyama says in an interview with Nakahira that this encounter prompted him to become "determined to negate the values that are attached to one single photograph."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Moriyama-2016-16):393 Moriyama photographed images reproduced from different mass media, including a television still of Lyndon B. Johnson announcing the suspension of the bombing of North Vietnam, newswire shots of Richard Nixon shortly after winning the presidential election, and the corpses of brutally killed Vietcong soldiers, along with the aforementioned image of Robert F. Kennedy.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Fukugawa-2012-15):464 Moriyama treated the camera as a device that copies reality and thus produces "equivalents," rendering insignificant the distance that the original photographs, the endlessly reproduced press images, and Moriyama's own versions have from the initial event.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Fukugawa-2012-15):465 The twelve-part series was published in _[Asahi Camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asahi\_Camera "Asahi Camera")_ alongside his own texts, where he describes the unpredictability of fate and the precariousness of human experience, believing that the camera has the capacity to reveal the "possibility of tragedy [that] has somehow seeped into the surrounding environment."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Charrier-2010-8):275

### _Shashin yo sayōnara_ (Farewell Photography) (1972)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daid%C5%8D_Moriyama&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Shashin yo sayōnara (Farewell Photography) (1972)")]

Published in April 1972, _Shashin yo sayōnara_ ("Farewell Photography") emerged within the context of Japan's aggressive cultural and economic revival—best exemplified in the creative sphere by [Expo '70](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expo_'70 "Expo '70")—and continued suppression of left-wing politics, as illustrated by the failure of the 1970 Anpo protests and the subsequent renewal of the [United States-Japan Security Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Mutual_Cooperation_and_Security_between_the_United_States_and_Japan "Treaty of Mutual Cooperation and Security between the United States and Japan").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Fukugawa-2012-15):470 The photobook, as suggested by the title, takes a [nihilistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihilism "Nihilism") turn from his prior work, turning its attention towards the incidental and evocative nature of photography rather than the visual subject itself.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Holborn-2004-7):74[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Charrier-2010-8):283 The images highlight the physical [detritus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detritus "Detritus") of the photographic process, such as the edges of discarded film, flecks of dust, and light leaks, along with the material dimensions of image-making as evidenced through the sprocket holes on negative strips and the brand names of the film, challenging the [indexical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indexicality "Indexicality") relationship between photographer, camera, and image and the established conventions of viewing photographs as referents of reality.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Holborn-2004-7):74[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Charrier-2010-8):283

### _Karyūdo_ (A Hunter) (1972)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daid%C5%8D_Moriyama&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Karyūdo (A Hunter) (1972)")]

Inspired by the liberatory and indeterminate qualities of Sal Paradise's journey in [Jack Kerouac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kerouac "Jack Kerouac")'s _[On the Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_the\_Road "On the Road")_ (1957, first Japanese translation published in 1959), Moriyama borrowed a friend's old Toyota and embarked on a solo [road trip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_trip "Road trip") across Japan, capturing photographs along the trip that would become the basis for _Karyūdo_ ("A Hunter"), a photobook published in June 1972 as the tenth installment of the series _Gendai no me_ ("The Modern Gaze").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-17) Many of the scenes were captured by Moriyama as he drove past them, made evident by the skewed angles, blurry, moving figures, and fragments of road infrastructure that cut across the picture plane. The title of the volume refers to his "stalker-life" attitude towards observing and capturing his surroundings, through the perspective of a cold, detached, solitary watcher. At the same time, the volume maintains a certain open-endedness in its format, lacking any sort of narrative resolution that might typically accompany the trope of a road trip or a hunting excursion, and instead putting forth a sensation of perpetual anxiety and uncertainty through its succession of consistently detached and irresolvable images of subjects and scenes across Japan.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Charrier-2010-8):289[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Mangione-18)

The book contains some of Moriyama's best-known images, including "Stray Dog, Misawa, 1971", which depicts a growling, haggard dog turning its head towards the camera. The image was taken in [Misawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misawa,_Aomori "Misawa, Aomori"), Aomori prefecture, where a large US Air Force base is located (Moriyama shot at other U.S. military bases throughout his career, including at the naval base in [Yokosuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Fleet_Activities_Yokosuka "United States Fleet Activities Yokosuka").)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Buruma-2018-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-20) The introduction of the book was written by pop artist and graphic designer [Tadanori Yokoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadanori_Yokoo "Tadanori Yokoo"), who wrote of Moriyama's pictures as being akin to "someone who talks, without looking people in the eye."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Charrier-2010-8):268 The book was re-released in 2011 with the addition of new commentary by Moriyama.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-21)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Mangione-18)

In 1974 Moriyama helped [Shōmei Tōmatsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sh%C5%8Dmei_T%C5%8Dmatsu "Shōmei Tōmatsu") to establish the _Workshop Photography School_ to teach their new understanding of photography to students. [Nobuyoshi Araki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobuyoshi_Araki "Nobuyoshi Araki"), [Eikoh Hosoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eikoh_Hosoe "Eikoh Hosoe"), [Masahisa Fukase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masahisa_Fukase "Masahisa Fukase") were also involved. They published a magazine, the _Workshop Quarterly,_ that reached eight issues. When the engagement broke up two years later, Moriyama and his students founded _Image Shop Camp,_ the first gallery in Japan dedicated exclusively to photography. In the eight years of their existence the around 30 members had organized 200 exhibitions, and "gave rise to some of the most explosive happenings in the history of post-war Japanese photography."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-22)

In 1974 the [National Museum of Modern Art in Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Modern_Art,_Tokyo "National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo") organized the photography exhibition _Fifteen Photographers Today,_ curated by Tsutomu Watanabe, who had selected Moriyama, Araki and Fukase alongside Shoko Hashimoto, [Kazuo Kitai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazuo_Kitai "Kazuo Kitai"), [Masatoshi Naito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masatoshi_Naito "Masatoshi Naito"), [Takuma Nakahira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takuma_Nakahira "Takuma Nakahira"), Takao Nikura, [Hajime Sawatari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajime_Sawatari "Hajime Sawatari"), [Kishin Shinoyama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kishin_Shinoyama "Kishin Shinoyama"), [Yutaka Takanashi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yutaka_Takanashi "Yutaka Takanashi"), [Shigeru Tamura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shigeru_Tamura_(photographer) "Shigeru Tamura (photographer)"), Katsumi Watanabe, Shuji Yamada, and [Shin Yanagisawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shin_Yanagisawa "Shin Yanagisawa").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-23)

Moriyama's work, though intimately engaged with the intricacies of social life and the image-laden nature of modern society, did not aspire to the same tendencies of social reportage exhibited by his contemporaries during the 1970s.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-24)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Buruma-2018-19) Instead, his approach takes into account the futility of the medium in reproducing the reality of his surroundings, the inherently fragmentary nature of the world, and the indelible presence of the photographer in all images, lurking or haunting the sphere of his subjects.

He has continued to shoot artistic as well as commercial work over the decades both in and outside of Japan, and is one of the most active and prolific contemporary photographers in Japan. In 2024, he photographed American rapper [Kanye West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanye_West "Kanye West")'s cover for his [studio album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_album "Studio album")_[Bully](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bully\_(album) "Bully (album)")_ (2026).

## Style and technique

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daid%C5%8D_Moriyama&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Style and technique")]

Influences cited by Moriyama include [Seiryū Inoue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seiry%C5%AB_Inoue "Seiryū Inoue"), [Eikoh Hosoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eikoh_Hosoe "Eikoh Hosoe"), [Shōmei Tōmatsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sh%C5%8Dmei_T%C5%8Dmatsu "Shōmei Tōmatsu"),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-25)[William Klein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Klein_(photographer) "William Klein (photographer)"), [Andy Warhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol "Andy Warhol"),[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-26)[Yukio Mishima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yukio_Mishima "Yukio Mishima"), and [Shūji Terayama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sh%C5%ABji_Terayama "Shūji Terayama").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-27)

The [Shinjuku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinjuku "Shinjuku") area is frequent setting for Moriyama's images of urban life. The photographer cites Shinjuku's shadowy, labyrinthine streets and alleys as a source of inspiration and allure, describing the area as having "a strange narcotic effect...something about it that traps me and puts me under a spell."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-28)

Moriyama predominantly presents his work in the form of photobooks (and self-published photo magazines), which he describes as open-ended sites, allowing the reader to decide on the sequence of images that they view.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-29) Since 1968, he has published more than 150 photobooks.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-30) The photobook arose as a popular format in the 1950s and 60s, and were often produced at a small scale and disseminated through bookstores and localized political networks rather than being mass-produced by major publishing houses.

Since the 2000s he has a preference for having a third party work on the formatting and recomposition of the images, as it frees him from the influences of his own memory and filters the images through the eye of an outsider.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Remix-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-32):24–27 A collection of Moriyama's writings, compiled from a fifteen-part series published in _Asahi Camera_ beginning in 1983, have been published as an autobiographical photobook titled _Inu no kioku_ ("Memories of a Dog").

Moriyama's photographs are often captured in a 4:5 [aspect ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspect_ratio_(image) "Aspect ratio (image)") rather than the 3:2 ratio associated with the [35 mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/135_film "135 film") format, and he has at times cropped his 35 mm photographs in order to achieve his preferred vertical format.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Fondation_Cartier_pour_l'Art_Contemporain-2003-33)

Moriyama tends to capture images without looking through the viewfinder, so as to separate himself from the detached, scientific, and deliberate cropping produced by the viewfinder lens. He often takes a large volume of photographs of the world as it passes by him, embracing the uncertainty and indeterminacy of encountering the scenes as they reveal themselves during the development process.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-world-through-my-eyes-10):210 Many of his works are also analogue composites, with many layered film frames used to create a single print.

### Color and digital work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daid%C5%8D_Moriyama&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Color and digital work")]

While Moriyama is most recognized for his black-and-white film photography, he has been shooting with color since the 1970s, and since the late 2000s has turned increasingly to compact digital photography, now working almost exclusively in this medium.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Nakamoto-2019-5):78–79 From time to time, he has also shot [Polaroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polaroid_Corporation "Polaroid Corporation") images, which he treats as "tiles" in installation settings, exhibiting them in groups rather than as discrete photographs.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Fondation_Cartier_pour_l'Art_Contemporain-2003-33)

In 1970, he helped produce the Asahi Journal's new color photography series _Dai go shōgen_ ("The Fifth Quadrant") and published photo essays on new development projects in Osaka and Tokyo, cherry blossoms in Osaka, and American military base towns in the [Kantō region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kant%C5%8D_region "Kantō region"). These projects employed his unconventional framing styles along with white balance and color exposure distortions that enhanced the uncanny, unsettling features of the world around him.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Charrier-2010-8):281

Due to his tendency to take a large number of shots when photographing, Moriyama finds the digital format more amenable to his needs, and rejects critics who fixate on the preciousness of film photography.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Nakamoto-2019-5):79 In response to a question posted by writer Takeshi Nakamoto's regarding Moriyama's advice for beginner street photographers, Moriyama states, "Get outside. It’s all about getting out and walking. That’s the first thing. The second thing is, forget everything you’ve learned on the subject of photography for the moment, and just shoot. Take photographs—of anything and everything, whatever catches your eye. Don’t pause to think."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Nakamoto-2019-5):11

_Daido Tokyo_ at [Fondation Cartier pour l’art Contemporain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fondation_Cartier_pour_l'Art_Contemporain "Fondation Cartier pour l'Art Contemporain"), Paris in 2016 was the first major solo show to display his color photographs.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Paik-34) Between 2008 and 2015, Moriyama revisited Tokyo, with a focus on the [Shinjuku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinjuku "Shinjuku") district—where much of his early career was spent—to take 86 chromogenic prints ("Tokyo Colour" series, 2008–2015) and black-and-white photographs ("Dog and Mesh Tights," 2014–2015).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Paik-34)

Moriyama's work has been not often but consistently featured in group and solo exhibitions in Japan since the mid-1970s, usually about two solo shows per year with his first in 1970 titled _Scandal._ With the series called _Pantomime_ he had his debut in 1968 together with [Shin Yanagisawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shin_Yanagisawa "Shin Yanagisawa") at Ginza Nikon Salon in Tokyo where he was exhibited again several times over the following years, while he showed his work at the _Image Shop Camp,_ too.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Biography/solo_exhibitions-35) In 1974 the _Printing Show_ took place at Shimuzu Gallery in Tokyo. Instead of photographs on the walls Moriyama printed a series of his photographs on a photocopy machine, shuffled them and then were staple-bound with silkscreened cover (visitors could choose between two), resulting in the photobook titled _Another Country._ (The event was restaged in 2011 at [Aperture Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aperture_Foundation "Aperture Foundation") in New York and the following year at the [Tate Modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Modern "Tate Modern") in London.)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-36)

Moriyama rose to prominence in the States after being heavily featured in the landmark group exhibition _New Japanese Photography_ at the [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art") in 1974, curated by [John Szarkowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Szarkowski "John Szarkowski") and [Shoji Yamagishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sh%C5%8Dji_Yamagishi "Shōji Yamagishi").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Museum_of_Modern_Art-1974-38) Selected as one of thirteen photographers in the show, Moriyama brought a grittier edge that emphasized the rawness of visual encounter, as well as a youthful perspective to the collection of artists, which included older practitioners such as [Ken Domon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Domon "Ken Domon") and [Shigeru Tamura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shigeru_Tamura_(photographer) "Shigeru Tamura (photographer)"), avant-garde contemporaries (and mentors to Moriyama) such as Shomei Tomatsu and Eikoh Hosoe, as well as those working in more polished, intellectualized, and observational approaches such as [Ken Ohara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Ohara "Ken Ohara"), [Ryoji Akiyama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ry%C5%8Dji_Akiyama "Ryōji Akiyama"), and [Bishin Jumonji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishin_Jumonji "Bishin Jumonji").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Museum_of_Modern_Art-1974-38)

In terms of solo exhibitions he was not recognized elsewhere until the mid-1990s; only a single show took place outside Japan, namely in Austrian [Graz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graz "Graz") in 1980 (after a group show of contemporary Japanese photography in 1977).[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Biography/solo_exhibitions-35) Since then the interest has accelerated and led to a number of major retrospectives. Beginning with the seminal 1999 retrospective exhibition _Daido Moriyama: Stray Dog_ at [San Francisco Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Museum_of_Modern_Art "San Francisco Museum of Modern Art") curated by [Sandra S. Phillips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandra_S._Phillips "Sandra S. Phillips"), that subsequently travelled to New York, Cambridge, and San Diego, as well as Switzerland and Germany.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-SFMOMA-1999-39) It was followed in 2003 by a retrospective that travelled through Japan and a first exhibition at the [Fondation Cartier pour l'art contemporain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fondation_Cartier_pour_l'art_contemporain "Fondation Cartier pour l'art contemporain") in Paris, where a follow-up was organized in 2016 (_Daido Tokyo_), for which he was commissioned to create an "immersive" multiscreen projection of black-and-white photographs (_Dog and Mesh Tights_).[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-40) Another major show travelled in 2007 from Cologne, Germany, to Seville, Spain and finally to the [Tokyo Metropolitan Museum of Photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Metropolitan_Museum_of_Photography "Tokyo Metropolitan Museum of Photography"). 2012 saw two institutional exhibitions at the [Los Angeles County Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_County_Museum_of_Art "Los Angeles County Museum of Art"),[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-Fracture:_Daido_Moriyama-41) and the [Tate Modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Modern "Tate Modern") (with [William Klein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Klein_(photographer) "William Klein (photographer)")).[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daido_Moriyama#cite_note-42)
